newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Slovakia says Hungary flouted Danube dam treaty.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia says Hungary flouted Danube dam treaty.

text.p: Slovakia accused Hungary on Monday of causing a long-running dispute over the diversion of the Danube's waters for a hydroelectric power project by failing to honour legally binding commitments under a bilateral treaty.
Foreign ministry lawyer Peter Tomka told the International Court of Justice that Hungary had invoked environmental concerns to obscure legal issues at the heart of the dispute.
"This is a treaty case. It primarily concerns Hungary's failure to carry out its obligations under the 1977 treaty," Tomka told the United Nations court.
He was speaking at hearings on the Gabcikovo dam project which provides 10 percent of Slovakia's electricity but has led to strained relations between Budapest and Bratislava.
The Slovak dam was originally part of a 1977 plan agreed by the then Communist governments of Czechoslovakia and Hungary.
But Hungary suspended work on a companion dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 after pressure from environmental groups, and in 1992 it pulled out of the project altogether.
Slovakia pressed ahead with the hydroelectric scheme at Gabcikovo after its split from Czechoslovakia in 1993 but it agreed to submit the dispute to the U.N. court.

It says Hungary broke its part of the agreement and should pay damages to Slovakia, arguing that Budapest made the environmental problems worse by halting construction of the Nagymaros dam which would have offset the effects of Gabcikovo.
Hungary, which presented its case earlier this month, says it abandoned the project because of concern about its effect on water supplies and the environment.
Reduced water flow and falling ground water levels, it says, have had a devastating effect on the flora and fauna of the Danube's flood plains as well as on agriculture and fisheries.
Hungarian delegation leader Gyorgy Szenasi accused Slovakia of pursuing its own economic interests at the expense of the environment by pressing ahead with the project on its own.
Szenasi said the plans to use the Danube's waters to generate power were a relic of the days when the neighbouring countries were both under Communist rule.
But Tomka said it was nonsense for Hungary to dismiss them as an "ill-conceived piece of socialist megalomania".
"The purpose of the 1977 treaty was not to build a monument to Socialist integration. It was to... provide electricity, flood control and improved navigation," he said.
He contrasted hydroelectric power as a clean source of energy compared with the nuclear and fossil-fuel plants recently built by Hungary to meet its power needs.
The International Court of Justice is the main judicial organ of the United Nations and settles disputes between states in accordance with international law.
The court's 15 judges will visit the Gabcikovo dam and view its alleged effects on the Hungarian side of the river in early April. They are expected to deliver their ruling in the autumn.
